title: CAP Theorem and Consistency Models
summary: A network partition forces a choice between rejecting operations and risking stale answers; normal operation has different tradeoffs.
body:
Picture two replicas separated by a failed network link. Both sides receive requests, but neither can confirm what the other side has accepted. This is the precise situation CAP describes, not a perpetual choice of any two attractive product features.

## What CAP actually says

- **Consistency** in CAP means a single-copy, linearizable view: once a write completes, subsequent reads behave as if there were one up-to-date copy.
- **Availability** means every request to a nonfailed node eventually gets a non-error response, not merely that the service meets a 99.9% uptime target.
- **Partition tolerance** means the system continues making its defined choice when messages between nodes are lost or indefinitely delayed.

A distributed system cannot wish away a network partition. During one, a CP design may reject or block requests on the side that cannot reach a quorum, preserving a single authoritative value. An AP design keeps answering on both sides, but may return stale values or accept concurrent writes that need reconciliation. Neither classification tells you every behavior of a database in every deployment. MongoDB's majority writes, Cassandra's tunable quorum, and Dynamo-style systems all have configuration and operation-specific behavior; do not assign a blanket guarantee from a brand name.

## Translate guarantees into user experience

A linearizable read after a successful bank transfer lets the user see the new balance, but contacting a leader or quorum can add cross-zone latency and may fail during partition. An eventually consistent replica might return the old balance briefly; it can serve a social feed well, but is not enough by itself to prevent spending the same balance twice. “Eventually” promises convergence once updates stop and communication resumes, not a fixed two-second deadline. Read-your-writes can be offered per session without making every global read linearizable.

| Operation | Likely choice | User-visible consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reserve the last seat | Reject if the authority is unreachable | No double booking; some users cannot reserve |
| Display a like count | Serve a reachable replica | Count may lag, but the feed remains responsive |

## Beyond the partition: PACELC

Most of the time there is no partition. PACELC adds the everyday choice: else, choose lower latency or stronger consistency. A cross-region synchronous confirmation improves read-after-write guarantees but adds a network round trip even on a healthy day. A local replica is faster yet may lag. Discuss the guarantee per operation rather than stamping “CP” or “AP” onto an entire architecture.

The obvious answer “choose two out of C, A, P” is wrong because P is not optional when a partition occurs; the meaningful decision is what to do during that failure and how much latency to spend otherwise.

## How to answer this in an interview

> For a ticket service with 10,000 seats, I would route each seat's reservation through a single authoritative shard and require a committed write before returning success. If its quorum is unreachable for 30 seconds, I would return an error for reservations rather than sell the same seat twice; seat-view counts can lag on replicas.
keyTakeaways: CAP constrains consistency versus availability during a partition; partitions are not an optional feature.
A CP operation may refuse requests; an AP operation may respond with stale data and need conflict resolution.
Linearizability gives a single-copy illusion; eventual consistency permits temporarily old answers.
PACELC exposes latency-versus-consistency costs even without a partition.
